posts.post_text: We banned ChatGPT in our analytics department last month. Not because AI is bad — because nobody could explain where the numbers came from. When a regulator asks 'how did you arrive at this figure?' and the answer is 'GPT said so', you've got a compliance problem. The AI trust gap is real and growing.
posts.angle: High-scoring compliance pain post with three ICP prospects engaging — validate the 'unexplainable output' problem and add the insight that auditability isn't a feature request, it's the whole game in regulated industries
posts.draft_comment: The 'GPT said so' answer is exactly where trust collapses — and in financial services it collapses fast. It's not really an AI problem, it's a lineage problem. If you can't trace a number back to a source a regulator can inspect, the output is basically useless no matter how accurate it looks. Curious whether you found the ban was enough, or whether it just pushed people toward less visible workarounds?

posts.post_text: We spent 18 months building a Power BI dashboard that our finance team refuses to use. They still export everything to Excel and email it around. The building part was easy. Getting people to actually trust the numbers enough to quote them in a board meeting? That's the real challenge nobody talks about. Anyone else hit this wall?
posts.angle: ICP prospect COO at 140-person consulting firm hitting the classic adoption wall — validate the trust problem specifically, add the insight that the dashboard isn't actually the product
posts.draft_comment: The 18 months wasn't wasted on the wrong tool — it was spent on the wrong problem. A dashboard nobody quotes in a board meeting is just a very expensive spreadsheet with better colours. The real product was never the viz, it was trust in the number and the story behind it. What did the finance team say when you asked them why they didn't trust it?

posts.post_text: Hot take: self-service BI is a myth. We gave everyone Power BI licenses and what happened? 200 reports, zero consistency, three different definitions of 'revenue'. The promise of democratising data is great until you realise nobody agrees on what the data means. Build vs buy isn't the question — it's 'who owns the truth?'
posts.angle: Innovation Director at NorthStar Retail is engaging with a post about BI chaos — validate the 'who owns truth' framing and add the insight that the tool is never the problem, the missing semantic layer is
posts.draft_comment: The 200 reports thing is so familiar it's almost a rite of passage. The tool works fine — the problem is there's no single place that says 'this is what revenue means here, full stop.' Everyone's just building on top of an unresolved argument. Who in your org is actually allowed to settle that definition when it's contested?

posts.post_text: AI hallucinations in analytics are a security issue, not just an accuracy issue. If your AI tool generates a financial report with hallucinated numbers and someone makes a decision based on it, that's not a bug — it's a material risk. We need to start treating AI outputs with the same scrutiny as we treat user inputs.
posts.angle: CISO raising AI hallucinations as a security risk with a CEO prospect engaging — validate the reframing, add the trust layer insight, no pitch
posts.draft_comment: The reframe from accuracy problem to security problem is exactly right — and I'd argue most analytics teams haven't caught up to that yet. The same orgs that would never ship user inputs without validation are happily putting AI-generated numbers in front of executives with zero audit trail. At some point the question isn't just 'is this number correct' but 'can anyone explain where it came from?' — and right now, most tools can't answer that.

posts.post_text: Had a fascinating conversation with a client yesterday. They spent £200k on a BI platform and the only person who can use it is the one who built it. Self-service my arse. The gap between what vendors promise and what actually happens in a 50-person company is enormous. When will the industry admit that most BI tools are built for data teams, not business teams?
posts.angle: ICP prospect (COO at Sterling Consulting) engaging with post about BI tools failing non-technical users — validate the £200k waste pain, add the 'built for builders not users' insight, no pitch
posts.draft_comment: That £200k number stings but it's not even the real cost — it's every decision that got made on gut feel because nobody could get a straight answer out of the thing. The dirty secret is most BI tools are basically very expensive ways to give analysts more work to do. The 'self-service' just means the business team has to find a friendlier analyst. What would it even look like if the tool was designed around the question, not the query?

posts.post_text: Just had our quarterly review and the CFO asked why the numbers in our BI dashboard don't match the numbers in the ERP. Turns out three different teams were applying different filters to the same dataset. AI won't fix this. Culture will. But nobody wants to hear that.
posts.angle: Commercial Director at a likely mid-market manufacturer surfacing a classic data trust problem — validate the culture diagnosis but add the nuance that tooling choices either make the culture problem worse or easier to contain
posts.draft_comment: Three teams, three filter interpretations — that's not a discipline problem, that's a system that made it too easy to go rogue. The culture argument is right, but culture is downstream of what the tools make the default behaviour. If filtering is hidden and individual, you'll always get this. The question is whether your BI setup rewards consistency or just rewards speed.

posts.post_text: Unpopular opinion: most operational dashboards are vanity projects. We had 47 KPIs on our ops dashboard. Nobody looked at it. Cut it to 5 metrics that actually drive decisions. Usage went from 10% to 85%. The problem with BI isn't the tools — it's that we measure everything and understand nothing.
posts.angle: ICP prospect (Director of Operations at Summit Group) engaging on dashboard overload — validate the 47-to-5 insight, add a layer on why usage actually dropped in the first place
posts.draft_comment: 47 KPIs isn't a dashboard problem, it's a 'nobody said no' problem. Every team adds their metric, nobody removes one, and eventually you've got a wall of numbers that tells a story nobody asked for. The jump from 10% to 85% usage is the real data point here — most ops leaders never even measure whether people look at the thing. What made you finally feel safe cutting it down to 5?

posts.post_text: Rolled out Copilot to 500 users last quarter. Usage after 90 days? 12%. The problem isn't the tool — it's that nobody knows what to ask it. We're essentially paying for a very expensive autocomplete. Shadow AI is the real story here — people are using ChatGPT on their phones because Copilot is too locked down.
posts.angle: IT Director exposing the adoption gap in enterprise AI rollouts — validate the shadow AI observation and reframe the real problem as data literacy, not tool access
posts.draft_comment: The shadow AI thing is the most honest part of this. People aren't going rogue because Copilot is bad — they're going rogue because they already know how to talk to ChatGPT and nobody ever taught them how to talk to their own data. Locking down the tool without solving that underlying problem just means you've spent the budget and still have the same gap. What's the plan for the 88%?
